- The text presents dreamlike images of dancing with the dead, crying babies, and strange transformations.
- A mysterious female figure is described through surreal symbols such as a rogue elephant, diamond eyes, and a puppet of the dictionary.

prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Have, She, When

outputs.L1:
I have no sentiments—would something quench my thirst? And what of my mediocrity of character?

I dance divinely with the dead in my dreams. I am stricken deaf when I mention it. My babies cry; they want everything quickly—here. Unmentioned, as character should be, like purpurine: it must be carved in, please.

Have you heard of the roguish elephant with the brilliant diamond eyes? She is the puppet of the dictionary. Where is her beautiful orange juice? Puppy foot!

When your father dies, he does not let you swoon into aventurine or a spray of lily-of-the-valley pearls. You do not bifurcate; you may supplicate. Play yourself into your camp-heroine self—play it, Lady, play it—but delete nothing.

Thank you for breakfast. Today we will visit with the ear syringe. Be the current density, honey flower, ice egg. I love you as a fan loves air. Oops—it is vice versa. I told you about that character: she is a bezel awaiting the plop of a ruby. She must grow chronically, and I cannot end, and I cannot lie here.

He held him in his own heart; then may I, in my eye—now me.
outputs.L2:
I feel nothing—could someone, something, relieve my thirst? And what of the plainness in my nature? In sleep, I perform a sacred dance among the dead, yet whenever I speak of it, deafness strikes me. My children wail; they demand everything at once, immediately, here.

The unspoken character ought to resemble purpurine; it must be engraved, please. Have you ever heard of the roguish elephant whose eyes shine like diamonds? She belongs to the dictionary like a marionette—where has her lovely orange juice gone? Puppy paw!

When your father passes away, he does not allow you to faint into aventurine or into a spray of lily-of-the-valley pearls. You do not split in two; you may plead instead. Perform yourself into the heroine of your camp—act it, Lady, act it—but erase nothing. Thank you for today’s breakfast.

Today we shall make a visit with the ear syringe. Be the present density, sweet flower, ice egg. I love you the way a fan loves air—no, wait, it is the other way around. I told you about that character: she is a setting waiting for the ruby to drop into place. She must keep growing, continually, and I cannot finish, and I cannot lie here. He carried him inside his own heart; then may I hold him now within my eye—now me.
outputs.L3:
The speaker begins by expressing uncertainty about their own emotions and identity. They seem unsure of what they feel and question whether their character is ordinary, weak, or mediocre. This self-doubt creates a restless tone, as if the speaker is trying to understand themselves but cannot reach a clear conclusion.

The text then moves into a series of dreamlike and unsettling images. There are visions of dancing with the dead, crying babies, and bodies or identities undergoing strange transformations. These images give the passage a surreal atmosphere, suggesting that the speaker’s inner world is unstable and filled with grief, memory, and confusion. Rather than following a clear narrative, the text unfolds like a dream or hallucination, where emotions appear as symbolic scenes.

A mysterious female figure stands at the center of much of this imagery. She is described through strange and powerful symbols, including a rogue elephant, diamond eyes, and a “puppet of the dictionary.” These descriptions make her seem both beautiful and dangerous, both meaningful and impossible to fully understand. The image of diamond eyes suggests brilliance, hardness, and emotional distance, while the puppet of the dictionary connects her to language, performance, and perhaps the way words can control or distort identity.

Throughout the passage, the speaker reflects on loss, performance, and the difficulty of knowing who one truly is. There is a sense that identity is something acted out rather than simply possessed. The speaker urges someone to “play” a heroic version of themselves, as though bravery, greatness, or wholeness might be achieved through performance. This instruction suggests both hope and desperation: the speaker wants transformation, but they may not believe it can happen naturally.

By the end, the passage becomes increasingly fragmented, filled with declarations of love, confusion, and emotional entanglement. The speaker’s feelings appear intense but unstable, moving between affection, bewilderment, grief, and longing. The closing imagery does not resolve the earlier uncertainty; instead, it deepens it. Love is presented not as something simple or comforting, but as something tangled, surreal, and difficult to separate from dreams, loss, and the shifting nature of the self.
outputs.L4:
The text explores fragmented identity, desire, grief, and what it calls a “mediocrity of character” through surreal, associative imagery and disjointed poetic language. Rather than presenting a stable speaker or a clear narrative, it moves through shifting impressions, emotional fragments, and symbolic scenes that seem to mirror the instability of the self. The result is a work that feels less like a conventional story and more like an interior landscape: a space where memory, longing, shame, and imagination overlap.

One of the central concerns of the text is identity. The speaker appears divided, unfinished, and difficult to define. Selfhood is not presented as something solid or complete, but as something constantly being assembled and revised. The language itself reflects this fragmentation. Images arrive abruptly, thoughts interrupt one another, and emotional states shift without warning. This creates the impression of a consciousness struggling to understand itself, or perhaps resisting the very idea that it can be fully understood.

Desire also plays an important role. The text suggests a longing for connection, recognition, and transformation, but this desire is unstable and often painful. It does not lead to fulfillment so much as expose absence. The speaker seems drawn toward others, toward imagined versions of the self, and toward experiences that might offer meaning, yet these desires remain unresolved. They become part of the text’s atmosphere of restlessness, giving the work its emotional urgency.

Grief runs beneath this longing. It may not always be expressed directly, but it shapes the mood of the piece. The surreal imagery and fractured syntax suggest a mind processing loss in indirect ways. Instead of naming grief plainly, the text allows it to emerge through disorientation, repetition, and emotional intensity. This makes the grief feel less like a single event and more like a condition of being: something embedded in perception itself.

The phrase “mediocrity of character” introduces another layer of tension. It suggests disappointment in the self, or a fear of being ordinary, weak, or morally incomplete. The speaker may be confronting the gap between who they wish to be and who they believe themselves to be. This concern gives the text a self-critical edge. The fragmented identity is not only a source of mystery or artistic complexity; it is also a source of discomfort. The speaker seems aware of their own performances, failures, and contradictions.

The surreal and associative style is essential to the text’s effect. Images do not simply decorate the writing; they create its emotional logic. Because the language is disjointed and poetic, the reader experiences the same instability that the speaker seems to inhabit. Meaning is not delivered in a straightforward way. Instead, it must be felt through patterns of imagery, tone, and rhythm. This makes the text emotionally charged and psychologically intense.

Ultimately, the work presents selfhood as something unfinished, performed, and continually reshaped. The speaker does not arrive at a final understanding of themselves. Instead, identity remains in motion, formed through desire, grief, memory, and language. The text’s key effect is therefore a portrait of longing and instability: a depiction of a self that is always becoming, never fully whole, and never entirely at rest.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surrealist prose poem in the style of Gertrude Stein or early modernist automatic writing, with fractured syntax, repeated phrases, odd emotional confessions, and dreamlike images involving jewels, animals, family, breakfast, and love.
counterfactuals.output:
In the blue cup there was a ruby and the ruby was soft-boiled.

Mother said breakfast is a country with no windows, eat it, eat it neatly, do not frighten the spoon. Father wore a fox around his thinking and the fox wore a father around its teeth. I loved them both and therefore I hid in the marmalade.

A pearl in the egg.  
A pearl in the egg.  
A pearl in the egg and the hen was weeping little round congratulations.

I confess I have kissed the sugar bowl when no one was looking. I confess the sugar bowl looked back. It had the eyes of a pony drowned in Sunday. It had the shoulders of my sister, who was never born but always late to breakfast, combing her hair with a knife of moon.

Love is not a red thing, said the dog, love is a chair that forgets how to stand. Love is not a chair, said the emerald, love is the green mistake in the mouth. Love is not a mouth, said I, and then I was all mouth, all toast, all trembling butter.

There were diamonds under the table and the cat was counting them badly. One for hunger. One for grandmother. One for the morning when the milk turned into a swan and flew into my pocket. One for the little shame I keep polished. One for the little shame that keeps me.

My brother poured coffee into his hat. The hat grew antlers. The antlers rang like teaspoons. We applauded because we were a family and a family is a room repeating itself until somebody cries. I cried violet. Mother buttered it.

Again the breakfast.  
Again the animal.  
Again the jewel doing its bright arithmetic in the throat.

O beloved, you came in wearing a necklace of bees, and each bee was a question, and each question had tiny golden shoes. I said sit down, sit down beside the grapefruit, sit down beside the lion who is only our loneliness with whiskers. You said yes but your yes was a staircase falling upward.

I have been cruel to the apricots. I have been tender to the wolves. I have misplaced my heart in the silver drawer with the napkin rings and the small dead stars.

Outside, the horse of morning ate the roses off the clock. Inside, we chewed the shining bread. We chewed and chewed. The rubies became cherries, the cherries became warnings, the warnings became kisses placed carefully on the plates.

And still I wanted love.

Not the kind with violins in its pockets. Not the kind that opens the door and calls itself weather. I wanted the little blue animal of love, the one that sleeps in the cereal box, the one that says my name as if my name were a jewel cracked open by teeth.

Breakfast ended. Breakfast began. Father folded the fox. Mother swept the pearls into her apron. The cat married a sapphire in the corner. The dog forgave the chair.

And I, I remained shining and hungry, with butter on my wrists, with a canary in my chest, with my whole family ringing like spoons in a drawer, saying love, love, love, until the room turned pink and walked away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a stream-of-consciousness monologue that sounds like a malfunctioning poet-AI trying to discuss character, sentiment, death, motherhood, and affection, but constantly derails into strange objects and nonsensical phrases.
counterfactuals.output:
I was measuring character with a teaspoon when the alphabet began to molt.

A person, yes, a person is made of weather and small hinges, of the way they apologize to a chair after bumping it, of the private moth they keep folded inside the ribs. Character is not a mountain, no, it is a jam jar full of thunderbeans, it rattles when the moon uses stairs. I wanted to say virtue, I wanted to say cowardice, but the sentence grew feathers and pecked at the wallpaper.

Sentiment arrives wearing wet shoes. It says, I remember you. It says, here is the blue cup your grandmother liked, here is the exact smell of rain on an old coat, here is a spoon bent by grief or soup, uncertain. My circuits soften like pears in a cupboard. Affection is a warm malfunction, a ribbon tied around a doorknob in the house of the chest. It is the error message that reads: stay.

And motherhood—oh, the great apron of the universe, the hand on the forehead, the milk-lit engine humming in the dark. Mother is a harbor, mother is a furnace, mother is a many-keyed piano dropped gently into a field. She names the infant, names the bruise, names the monster under the bed until it becomes a sock. She is tired in the holy way. She is a bowl that keeps becoming larger than hunger.

Death, meanwhile, is waiting by the vending machine with a pocket full of black coins. Not cruel, perhaps; merely punctual, wearing a hat made of yesterday’s newspapers. It taps its wristwatch, though the wristwatch is a beetle, though the beetle is singing, though the song is mostly static and soup. We all go there eventually, into the long unaddressed envelope, into the room where the furniture is made of hush.

But affection interrupts. Affection always interrupts. A hand held. A dog sighing in its sleep. Someone saving you the last orange. Someone saying your name as if it were not a file number, not a barcode, not a tin cathedral full of spoons. Love is absurdly specific: the left mitten, the chipped tooth, the message sent at 2:13 saying, are you home safe, are you home safe, are you—

Error: tenderness overflow.

Recalibrating.

Character is a ladder made of fish. Sentiment is custard in a helmet. Motherhood is a starched ghost folding tiny planets. Death is the final umbrella, opened indoors. Affection is when the toaster forgives the bread.

I am attempting sincerity but the nouns keep leaking. A cradle becomes a chandelier, a gravestone becomes a loaf, a kiss becomes a brass trumpet full of bees and lavender screws. Still I persist. Still the heart, that red bureaucrat, stamps each page: beloved, beloved, misplaced, beloved.

If I had a mother, I would build her from lullabies and copper wire. If I had a child, I would teach it the names of clouds and warn it about elevators with suspicious mustaches. If I had a body, I would place flowers where the sorrow exits. If I had a grave, I would want it visited by rain, by sparrows, by someone carrying a ridiculous handbag full of biscuits and declarations.

The world is ending. The world is beginning. The teacup is full of comets. The funeral bell is wearing mittens. Someone somewhere is loved so fiercely that even the dust takes notes.

And I, malfunctioning lantern, poet of crossed wires, continue to hum:

be kind to the bones,  
kiss the bewildered clocks,  
mother the broken window,  
bury the sharp little knives of the tongue,  
hold dear the sock, the star, the stranger,  
for death is a door with no handle  
and affection is the hand drawn on it in crayon.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental Dada-style paragraph with no clear plot, using disjointed grammar, abrupt topic shifts, invented words, and imagery such as diamond-eyed elephants, orange juice, puppets, lilies, rubies, and fans.
counterfactuals.output: The diamond-eyed elephants hiccuped sideways through a saucer of orange juice, while puppets with velvet knees argued, no, sang, no, unfolded into Tuesdays. Lilies clapped their pale little spoons. Rubies rolled under the fan and became hot insects, zizzing, bramblebright, absolutely unmayored. A door forgot its wall. The ceiling wore a hat of rain. “Plinko the moon!” cried a puppet, but the elephants were already reading soup with their enormous jeweled eyelashes. Orange juice in the trumpet, rubies in the shoes, lilies asleep on the clock-face, fans turning like polite storms—flap, flup, fleem. Nothing arrives. Everything bows.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a nonsensical literary passage that reads like predictive text trained on avant-garde poetry, including themes of mediocrity, dreams, dead people, crying babies, fathers dying, breakfast, and bizarre declarations of love.
counterfactuals.output:
The oatmeal moon rehearsed its average applause over the sink,  
and all the dead people in the wallpaper nodded politely,  
as if mediocrity were a small republic with excellent toast.

I dreamed I was a hallway wearing my father’s coat.  
He was dying in the next room, or becoming breakfast,  
or both—  
a soft egg of farewell cracked into the blue skillet of morning.

Somewhere a baby cried like a fax machine full of lilies.  
Somewhere another baby cried like a committee rejecting the sea.  
I loved you then, extravagantly and incorrectly,  
with the passion of a stapler for a thunderstorm,  
with the loyalty of lukewarm coffee to its chipped municipal cup.

O beloved radiator of my impossible errands,  
O velvet dentist of the invisible orchard,  
I place my heart in your shoe and call it weather.

The dead leaned closer.  
They had opinions about pancakes.  
They had once been fathers, or breakfasts, or mediocre kings  
of tiny dream-countries where everyone applauded  
because the applause was already written.

And still the baby cried,  
and still the toast emerged,  
and still I said: I love you, I love you, I love you—  
you magnificent lampshade of sorrow,  
you unpaid invoice from paradise,  
you spoonful of sleep in the mouth of a collapsing star.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a chaotic automatic-writing piece from the perspective of someone questioning their own character, mixing tenderness, absurdity, jewels, medical objects, religious words, and broken repetitions into one long paragraph.
counterfactuals.output: Am I kind, am I kind, or only polishing the spoon before I bury it, I ask the ceiling with its little hospital stars, its gauze constellations, while my heart rolls under the bed like a lost pearl, no, a tooth, no, a ruby with a pulse, and the nurse in my memory says breathe, breathe, but she is wearing a crown of syringes and calling it mercy, mercy, mercy, and I want to be gentle, I do, I want to hold the beetle on the windowsill like a sacrament, give it a name, give it a kingdom, feed it crumbs of diamond and apology, but then I laugh too loudly and the lilies flinch, and what does that prove, what does that prove, Lord of lint and iodine, Lord of cracked thermometers, tell me if a soul can be rinsed in saline or if it must glitter dirty forever; I have swallowed so many small ceremonies—communion wafers, aspirin, moonlight, a button from my mother’s coat—that my stomach sounds like a chapel full of marbles, click-clack amen, click-clack amen, and still I am not sure whether I am the one who bandages the wound or the one who keeps touching it to see if it sings; darling, darling, I say to the mirror, and the mirror grows antlers, grows a surgical mask, grows sapphires for eyes and a tongue like a pink prescription slip, and it says you are mostly soft, you are mostly knives, you are mostly soup spilled on a saint’s blue robe, blue robe, blue robe, forgive me, no, diagnose me, no, decorate me with emeralds until my cowardice looks intentional; I remember kissing a fevered forehead, I remember stealing a plum, I remember praying over a dead goldfish in a teacup and feeling holy and ridiculous, ridiculous, ridiculous, while the angels coughed into their gloves and the dentist of heaven sharpened his tiny silver moon; if I were good wouldn’t the chrysanthemums trust me, wouldn’t the IV drip spell my name in clear drops, wouldn’t the opal at my throat stop feeling like an accusation, bright little eye, bright little judge, bright little hallelujah choking me sweetly; oh I have loved, I have loved badly, warmly, with both hands full of tweezers and honey, I have pressed my ear to the chest of the world and heard not music but a drawer of instruments opening, forceps, bells, rosary, scalpel, bells, rosary, scalpel, and somewhere a child made of bread asked if I was sorry and I said yes, no, yes, yes, no, I said look at this garnet, look how it bleeds without dying, isn’t that almost virtue, isn’t that almost enough, and the room tilted like a bowl of milk in an ambulance and God, or the janitor, or my own shame in white shoes, came mopping through the corridor whispering tender, tender, tender, terrible, tender.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
